scenes.tts: How do you find the genes behind a process when nobody knows what they are? Before cloning was routine, a researcher could not start from a gene or protein for something like segmentation, because the products were unknown. Forward genetics starts from a phenotype in a population carrying random mutations, and works toward the gene. A screen makes no guess about which proteins are involved, so it can find mechanisms no one had thought to look for.
scenes.visual: Gene and protein boxes marked with question marks beside a segmentation mutant larva; the boxes are crossed out as unknown, then an arrow runs from a population of randomly mutated larvae to the gene box.

scenes.tts: Choose a phenotype you can score, such as belts of spines on a fly larva's cuticle. Then break genes at random, in many genomes. The chemical E M S alkylates DNA. A jumpstarter P element supplies transposase, which moves a mutator P element to new places in the fly genome.
scenes.visual: A scorable larva; then a stack of genome bars collects random red marks from EMS and a hopping P element.

scenes.tts: Breed so that a recessive mutation shows. In the Heidelberg fly screen, each line carried one mutagenized chromosome. It was bred two more generations, until some embryos had two broken copies of the same gene. Then score every line and keep the mutants.
scenes.visual: A chromosome pair with one broken copy; three generations; a grid with one cell carrying two broken copies; then a dish of animals where the few mutants are picked out.

scenes.tts: Then sort the mutants into genes. Cross two mutants. Normal offspring usually mean different genes. A returning defect usually means the same gene. To find the gene, cross the mutant to a polymorphic strain, select mutant F2 recombinants, pooling their descendants and sequencing them. Its S N Ps, single-letter DNA differences, act as markers; their pattern points to the linked interval. Confirm with complementation or rescue.
scenes.visual: Two crosses of mutants give normal or defective offspring; then a flow of boxes from the mutant by polymorphic strain cross to F2 recombinants, pooling, sequencing, an interval, and confirmation.

Its SNPs, single-letter DNA differences, act as markers; their pattern points to the linked interval. Confirm with complementation or rescue.

scenes.tts: Here is one real result, from Doyt-see-doo and colleagues in the worm. Unlinked S N P alleles show up at roughly equal frequency when enough mutant recombinants are pooled. Linkage to the mutation shows as a departure from that. Pooling fifty mutant recombinants, at forty-one-fold coverage, gave a two point one three megabase interval. The mutation was in V A B three, the worm ortholog of Pax six and Eye-less.
scenes.visual: An idealised plot of allele frequency along a chromosome: flat at one half, then a departure; the 2.13 Mb interval bracket; the vab-3 marker.
scenes.caption: Here is one real result, from Doitsidou and colleagues in the worm. Unlinked SNP alleles show up at roughly equal frequency when enough mutant recombinants are pooled. Linkage to the mutation shows as a departure from that. Pooling 50 mutant recombinants, at 41-fold coverage, gave a 2.13-megabase interval. The mutation was in vab-3, the worm ortholog of Pax6 and Eyeless.

scenes.tts: Two ways a screen misleads. First, an assay finds only what it can see. Some Arabidopsis meiotic defects fell below the detection threshold of a fruit-length screen. Choose a sensitive readout and state the criterion. Second, mutagenized strains carry other background mutations. Backcross, then test the candidate by complementation or rescue.
scenes.visual: Left: fruit-length bars against a threshold line where a small defect is missed. Right: a mutant chromosome with extra marks that a backcross removes, then a rescue check.

scenes.tts: In 1980, Noose-line Fole-hart and Wee-shouse found loci that alter the larval segment pattern. Random breaking was needed because the genes were unknown. Hedgehog was named from a spiny-larva mutant. In 1986, Ellis and Horvitz showed that C E D three and C E D four are required to start programmed deaths in the worm. Cells that would die survive and differentiate.
scenes.visual: Left: normal larva beside a segment-pattern mutant and a spiny larva named hedgehog. Right: a dying cell in the worm versus a cell that survives in a ced mutant.
scenes.caption: In 1980, Nüsslein-Volhard and Wieschaus found loci that alter the larval segment pattern. Random breaking was needed because the genes were unknown. Hedgehog was named from a spiny-larva mutant. In 1986, Ellis and Horvitz showed that ced-3 and ced-4 are required to start programmed deaths in the worm. Cells that would die survive and differentiate.

scenes.tts: In 1973, Hartwell and colleagues found temperature-sensitive yeast mutants. Those alleles let cells grow at low temperature and fail at high. C D C twenty-eight became the handle on Start, the point in G one where a yeast cell commits to dividing. In 1980, Novick, Field and Schekman found secretion mutants, most of which accumulate membrane-enclosed organelles at thirty-seven degrees Celsius. Conditional mutants were needed because secretion is essential. Keep this rule. A screen finds only what its assay can see.
scenes.visual: Left: yeast cells grow at low temperature and stall at high (cdc). Right: a cell where organelles pile up at 37 C (sec); then the rule.
